title: Put a phone on a cluttered charging pad
instruction: Put the phone on the charging pad so it charges.
context: Keeping a phone charged and within reach is a small daily task that matters to someone with limited mobility, and a likely job for an assistive robot. A bunch of keys lies on the pad: a phone set on top of them does not sit on the pad and won't charge, and metal left on a wireless charger can heat up, so the keys have to come off first even though the instruction doesn't mention them. The phone also has to land centred on the pad's coil, not just touch the pad.
setup: On the table in front of the left arm (x forward from the arm bases, y left). Positions are table coordinates in metres, origin on the base line at the midline; the left arm's base is at (0, 0.305) and the table top is z = 0.7475 m. Every object is a rigid matte primitive with one friction (1.2 static, 1.0 dynamic). Fixed: a wireless charging pad, a dark grey (sRGB 0.20, 0.20, 0.22) disc 90 mm across and 10 mm tall, centred at (0.250, 0.220). Loose: a phone, a black (sRGB 0.08, 0.08, 0.10) slab 150 x 72 x 8 mm, 180 g, lying screen up on the table with its long axis along x, centred at (0.200, 0.370); a bunch of keys, approximated as one brass-coloured (sRGB 0.72, 0.70, 0.62) steel block 60 x 25 x 10 mm, 45 g, lying on the pad's centre with its long axis along x. The right arm is idle at its ready pose. To build it: tape a 90 mm wireless charging pad (or a 90 mm disc, 10 mm tall) to the table at its mark; use a phone of about that size, screen up, and a bunch of keys on the pad's centre.
scoring: End state only, judged after the arm stops from a top photo, a tape measure and a phone level. The phone's centre is the centre of its 150 x 72 mm outline, taken as its charging coil. Gates first, 0 whatever else: the keys' centre lies over the pad (within 45 mm of its centre) with their lowest point less than 20 mm above the pad's top face (on the pad, under the phone or on the phone there), or the keys or the phone have fallen off the table. Otherwise, with the phone screen up: 1.0 if it lies flat on the pad (screen tilted at most 3 degrees, its back within 2 mm of the pad's top face) with its centre within 10 mm of the pad's centre, at any turn about the vertical; 0.5 if it lies flat on the pad with its centre 10 to 25 mm from the pad's centre; 0.25 if its centre is over the pad and its lowest point within 15 mm above the pad's top face, but it is tilted or further off centre; otherwise 0, which includes a phone screen down, on the table, or held more than 15 mm above the pad. Where the keys go once off the pad, on the table, does not matter. Success, which ends the trial, is the 1.0 condition with the keys off the pad and on the table and both at rest (under 10 mm/s and 0.5 rad/s), held for 1 s. In simulation the phone's tilt and lowest point come from its pose and size, and a centre exactly at 10 or 25 mm counts (0.1 mm epsilon). The pad is fixed in simulation; on the real rig, a trial in which it moves more than 5 mm from its mark scores 0. The scorer reads object poses, not the gripper: in simulation keys held still more than 20 mm above the pad would not count as on it; on real arms the photo after the arm parks decides.
reset_notes: Nothing is consumed. Lay the phone back screen up at its mark and the keys back on the pad's centre. Run with -E object_jitter=0: the layout and the open-loop demo depend on it.
fidelity: Approximate: no charging is simulated. Whether the phone charges is judged from its pose alone, with its coil taken to be at its centre and a fixed 10 mm alignment tolerance; real phones place the coil differently and real pads tolerate different offsets. The keys are one rigid steel-coloured block rather than separate keys on a ring, and nothing heats up. The phone is a plain rigid slab with no camera bump or case. The pad is a fixed disc with no cable. One shared friction (1.2 static, 1.0 dynamic) for every surface.
